title: What diffraction means
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can describe progressive wavefronts and stationary-wave experiments, including fixed spatial maxima and minima.
new_learning: Recognise spreading through a gap or around an obstacle.
not_yet_taught: how diffraction depends on gap width compared with wavelength

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

blocks.title: Why can a wave reach behind a corner?
content: Imagine straight water wavefronts meeting a barrier with one opening. If waves only travelled straight ahead, the region beside the opening would stay calm. Instead, wavefronts can enter that side region.
The wave has spread beyond the straight-through path. We need a name for that change.

figure.purpose: Create the need for diffraction using a geometric-shadow puzzle.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper top view of straight water wavefronts approaching a barrier gap, with a lightly shaded geometric-shadow region behind the barrier and curved emerging fronts entering it. No definition text.
figure.alt_text: Water waves pass through a gap and spread into the region behind the barrier.

blocks.title: The name for spreading

controlled_definition.displayed_content: the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle

content: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle.
The definition has two essential ideas: spreading, and a gap or obstacle. Merely passing through an opening is not enough unless the wave changes direction into a wider region.

figure.purpose: Tie both branches of the controlled definition to clear spatial examples.
figure.brief: Two hand-drawn panels: wavefronts spreading through a gap and wavefronts bending around the edge of an obstacle. Use arrows to show newly reached directions.
figure.alt_text: Waves spread through a gap and around the edge of an obstacle.

blocks.title: Wavefronts reveal the spreading
content: Before the gap, several points on one wavefront move forward together. At the opening, the transmitted wave reaches directions that were not on the original straight route. Draw the emerging wavefront wider or curved to show this.
Around an obstacle edge, part of the wave continues into the region that straight rays would miss. This is the same core idea, now caused by an edge rather than a complete gap.

figure.purpose: Teach how wavefront diagrams encode spreading rather than reflection or absorption.
figure.brief: Before-and-after wavefront sequence with incoming parallel fronts, barrier edge, outgoing curved fronts and sparse direction arrows. Include a crossed-out straight-only continuation as a misconception cue.
figure.alt_text: Parallel wavefronts become curved and reach new directions after an edge.

blocks.title: Light at a narrow slit
content: Light passing through a narrow slit can reach positions outside the simple straight-line image of the slit. The light has spread after the aperture, so the event includes diffraction.
Do not explain bright and dark fringes yet. Those patterns require later interference ideas. In this lesson, the relevant observation is simply that light spreads beyond the straight-through region.

figure.purpose: Transfer the meaning of diffraction from water waves to light without introducing interference.
figure.brief: White-paper ray-and-wavefront sketch of a beam at one slit and a screen showing a broad reached region. Do not draw or label fringes.
figure.alt_text: Light through a slit reaches a wider region of a screen than a straight-only model predicts.

blocks.title: Spreading is not the wave turning into another wave
content: A common idea is that the barrier pushes the whole wave sideways. That feels natural because the path bends near the edge. It fails because different parts of the emerging wave travel into several directions, not one new direction.
Another useful picture is sound heard around a doorway. The sound remains sound, but the wave has spread into a region without a direct straight path from the source.

figure.purpose: Correct the single-sideways-turn misconception with a multi-direction comparison.
figure.brief: Comparison sketch: crossed-out single bent arrow versus several curved wavefronts spreading through a doorway toward a listener around the corner.
figure.alt_text: Diffraction spreads a wave into several directions rather than turning it along one path.

blocks.title: A two-part recognition test
content: First locate a gap or obstacle edge. Then ask whether the wave spreads into directions beyond the straight-ahead region. If both are present, diffraction is the right description.

Diffraction is different from the fixed maxima and minima of a stationary wave. A stationary pattern comes from superposition of opposite waves. Diffraction describes spreading at a boundary. How the amount of spreading changes with gap width and wavelength belongs to the next lesson.

figure.purpose: Summarise recognition and distinguish diffraction from prior stationary-wave evidence.
figure.brief: Two-column hand-drawn sorter: diffraction has gap/edge plus spreading; stationary wave has fixed maxima/minima. Use simple icons, no later ratio comparisons.
figure.alt_text: A visual sorter distinguishes diffraction spreading from a stationary-wave pattern.

misconceptions_addressed: Passing through any opening without spreading is enough to show diffraction.
A diffracted wave turns into one new direction.
Diffraction and stationary-wave patterns are the same phenomenon.
skills_students_can_now_use: State the controlled definition of diffraction.
Identify diffraction at a gap or obstacle from wavefront spreading.
next_lesson_can_assume: Diffraction is recognised as spreading at a gap or obstacle.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: dependence on gap width relative to wavelength
